To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the price volatility in real-time pricing can be characterized in term of the maximal relative price elasticity and that it increases as the relative price elasticity increases, i.e. the ratio between the price elasticity of demand and the price elasticity of supply.

the price volatility can be increased by the introduction of real-time retail pricing, and that this increase can be characterized by the ratio of the generalized elasticity of demand to that of generation.

real-time pricing in power grids with distributed generation can lead to increased volatility, and that the volatility can be characterized by the ratio of the maximal relative price-elasticities of consumers to that producers.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: (i) How does real-time pricing change the system's dynamics and the system's ability to respond to uncertainty?
the design of a power system with a real-time market that can be robust to uncertainty and volatility.
the analysis of power systems under real-time retail pricing with information asymmetry.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
real-time pricing is not necessarily bad. It depends on the system architecture and on the system parameters.
real-time pricing is not a panacea for power system problems, and that it should be used in a carefully designed and well understood framework.
the paper presents a novel and important contribution to the literature on real-time pricing in power systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the paper shows that the system can be more robust and more volatile at the same time.
the real-time retail pricing can increase volatility and reduce robustness of the system.

the system is more sensitive to demand and generation uncertainties when there is a direct feedback from prices to demand and supply, and that such a system is more volatile when demand and supply are less elastic to price changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the system's price-elasticity can be a useful measure for assessing the volatility of a power system under real-time pricing.
the architecture of the power system, including its market design, can have a significant impact on the system's volatility and robustness.
, in the presence of uncertainty, a closed-loop feedback control system may not be the most robust solution to the problem of increasing the price-elasticities of demand and generation.
